Content:
The 35c bribe reminded me of a news story from the Prohibition era that I read.
A patron had handed two dollars to a bartender (obviously intending to buy liquor), but when quizzed by prohibition agents, he panicked and said that he was actually buying sandwiches.
The bartender played along in an attempt to get the agents to leave, trying to convince them that he was "a regular who ate a lot of sandwiches."
After watching this poor guy eat thirteen sandwiches, the agents then produced their search warrants and found the illegal liquor they were looking for.

I just love old-timey stories involving what is now considered trivial amounts of money.

Content: I remember when butcher box or maybe it was a service that was similar with a similar name was new and they did door to door stuff in my area. I had never seen a door to door salesperson in real life and thought they'd show up in suits and talk in the cross Atlantic accent like in old shows. They did not. The meat salesman looked like a lumberjack, and the vacuum saleswoman dressed like my grandmother, specifically the boring one. It was especially confusing because we ended up not going with either and the meat guy was real chill about it despite being able to see our smoker and the vacuum lady was really pushy despite my mom being able to prove the vacuum we had already worked better right infront of her. I grew up poor so I always kept an eye out for sales on meats, being the kid who preferred grilled or smoked meat for every meal over literally any other foods. Now I let my stepdsd know a week in advance when pork prices are about to drop every year. For anyone wondering, pork prices drop the week before fall starts because everyone wants a spiral ham and like no other cuts and picks back up the week after new years, and a lot of people believe that's why McDonald's brings back the mcrib every year in the fall

Author: @LloydsofRochester
Content:
Just a thought, and only that because I haven't made this yet, but for the nutmeg, why not add a small amount of the mixture to the nutmeg in a small bowl to make a small paste and then put it in the eggnog mixture? EDIT: Made it, and adding a spoon or two of the egg mixture to the nutmeg makes a paste that mixes in easier. 

I don't drink hard liqour much so I don't know about flavors and didn't want to ruin it, but I do like Bailey's, and used 3 cups. Works! It also made it even more creamy.

I also used duck eggs...they have a lower percentage of whites to yolks and do not separate from the yolks (very creamy and rich) easily, so I'm not suggesting them. But I had 7, then added 3 chicken eggs for more whites (interestingly, those are more yellow), and added a little alum to help them whip better. They were soft-firm and I like it. It's now resting in a very large sealed bowl until Christmas in my unheated winter larder/summer pantry.

Content:
Last month was visiting my parents and my dad asks if I want eggnog
It wasn’t event Thanksgiving and I commented “already bought a bottle?” And he says no, it’s from the batch he made last year. 
I expressed concern that it was a year old and he assured me it tastes just fine, the everclear keeps
Me: oh…it’s Oma’s recipe 😂
Had a small glass. It was in fact amazing. So thick compared to store bought eggnog. But good gracious, make it a small glass!
 
My grandmother made notoriously STRONG eggnog. After sampling a glass my dad proceeded to lament how he needed to go drive to Virginia to get (and I quote) the ‘good everclear’ for Oma’s eggnog. 
And this is why we use tiny glasses at family gathering 😂

Content: As per Maitre d' Ficklin who is in charge of the White House Eggnog and has held that position for 42 years.  He saves four to five gallons of eggnog each year and stores it, sealed in the refrigerator.  The alcohol ensures that nothing will spoil, and truly mellows out over the year. Author: @TheStraycat74
Content:
Dr. Rebecca Lancefield's Eggnog Recipe

This recipe comes from Dr. Rebecca Lancefield (1895 – 1981), a prominent microbiologist who worked at The Rockefeller University. One of her perhaps lesser-known legacies is related to eggnog: every year, she would make eggnog in the lab before Thanksgiving, let it "mellow," and then serve it at Christmas. Forty years later, the eggnog tradition persists in that laboratory.

    1 dozen eggs
    1 quart heavy cream
    1 quart light cream
    1 pint bourbon
    1 quart rum
    nutmeg
    sugar to taste (1/2 - 3/4 lb)

Add the light cream with stirring. Add the sugar to taste with mixing (1 pound/batch), then add nutmeg to taste.

Leave standing at least overnight with lid slightly ajar in refrigerator. Serve after 2-3 weeks in the cold.

Different times...

Content:
🔔 MAX: Overcoming Egg White Allergy

Egg white allergy is a common food allergy that requires careful management to avoid severe reactions. 

Here’s a step-by-step guide to help you overcome egg white allergy...

1. Avoid Egg Whites and Products Containing Them

Read food labels carefully to identify hidden sources of egg whites, such as:

Baked goods (cakes, cookies, pastries)

Mayonnaise

Custards

Ice cream

Meringues

Marshmallows

Some sauces and dressings

Be cautious of cross-contamination in food preparation, cooking, and storage.

2. Identify Safe Alternatives

Choose egg-free products, such as:

Vegan or egg-free baked goods

Plant-based mayonnaise and sauces

Coconut-based or rice-based ice cream

Gelatin or agar agar as egg substitutes

Consult with a healthcare provider or registered dietitian for personalized recommendations.

3. Manage Symptoms and Reactions

Carry an EpiPen or other epinephrine auto-injector with you at all times.

Administer epinephrine immediately if symptoms of anaphylaxis occur (e.g., difficulty breathing, rapid heartbeat, swelling).

Seek medical attention promptly after administering epinephrine.

4. Consider Immunotherapy

If your egg white allergy is severe or persistent, consult with an allergist about immunotherapy (allergy shots).

Immunotherapy can help desensitize you to egg whites, reducing the risk of severe reactions.

Author: @ronsandahl274
Content: One note: If you are making an 1800's eggnog and only letting it sit for "three or four days" you are doing the nog a criminal injustice.  These nogs need AT MINIMUM three weeks.  When I make one (I highly recommend the Fanny Farmer recipe) I make it just after Thanksgiving, and then gently stir it once a week as it quickly settles.  The difference in waiting three weeks its that you will have the smoothest, silkiest, deadliest nog you have ever had.  One last note - if you want heavenly light eggnog, you should also whip 1/2 of the heavy cream.  You can whip more, but keeping at least some of the heavy cream liquid will help the nog not to separate too quickly.

Perhaps the Dutch 'advocaat' is more suitable for your egg white allergy. It's a custardy thick 'drink' of only egg yolks, sugar and brandy with an alcohol percentage of around 15%. Usually served in a small liqueur glass (fancy: with a dollop of whipped cream on top) and eaten with a small spoon. Also very nice as a 'sauce' on vanilla ice cream, with some dark chocolate shavings and whipped cream.
Due to the eggs, it's considered more of a Easter fancy drink/dessert, but many people also drink eat this around Christmas.

Author: @susanmercurio1060
Content:
Sounds just like the eggnog my mother used to make, except she used a dozen eggs: Beat egg yolks with sugar in a warm bowl until they turn pale yellow. Mix in one cup each of brandy, rum, and whiskey. Stir well to incorporate. Add 1 gallon of whole milk. Use a clean bowl and beat egg whites until they are light and fluffy (do not overbeat.) Beat 1 pint of heavy cream in a cold bowl, adding sugar and vanilla, until stiff peaks form. Fold whipped cream into the beaten egg whites. Fold this mixture into the eggnog base .
Sprinkle generously with grated nutmeg.

Author: @nikkiewhite476
Content:
Wooooot drinking history lives! 
Thanks Max and Jose this episode is awesome! 

Moose milk is a Canadian armed forces drink that I was blessed to have once. My mom made it for Christmas at least twice. I remember my dad asking her to make it but she said she didn't have time. A few years later after they had separated Mom made it again. I remember that it used two kinds of rum, light and dark, milk, cream and ice cream. I have tried to find a recipe but none do it like my mom did. They mix everything together and serve it the same day if not immediately. The way my mom made it was vastly different. 
You take a bottle each of dark rum and light rum, 4 L of milk and I think 2 L of cream. Mix those all together and put them into a gallon glass jar, the big ones you buy pickles in bulk in, put the jars in the fridge. Everyday you have to go shake the jars, for two weeks! Then you serve it over ice cream. 
You said waiting a day or two mellows the flavor of the booze, think about how smooth it gets after 2 weeks! I had two cups it was so very good, if I had not seen my mom making it I would have never guessed it had any alcohol. Just from those 2 cups I got quite drunk it is so potent. I should ask her for the full recipe because none of the recipes I saw while searching were like Mom's.

Author: @HylianSoldier64
Content:
Expanded on with GPT - Twas the night before Christmas, and all through West Point, 
all the students were wasted, about to tear up the joint.
The halls were all buzzing with whispers and dread,
Of the great eggnog riot that lay just ahead. 

With cups full of nog, spiked heavily with cheer,
The cadets gathered round, their tempers were clear.
They’d planned for this moment, the holiday plight,
But soon it would spiral into chaos that night. 

The officers warned them, “Behave or you’ll pay!”
But the promise of eggnog led them astray.
With a shout and a cheer, they began to revolt,
The drunken cadets had lost all control. 

The mugs were all tossed, the air filled with noise,
As brawls broke out amongst West Point’s young boys.
A punch here, a kick there, the snow stained with drink,
A riot ignited, quicker than you'd think. 

The officers tried, but their orders were drowned,
As cadets ran riot, all over the ground.
Eggnog splattered, the barracks in flames,
The campus was chaos, no one was tame. 

Then through the mayhem, there arose such a sound,
The jingle of sleigh bells, the hooves on the ground.
Saint Nicholas appeared, with a scowl on his face,
"Enough of this madness, calm down in this place!" 

But the cadets were wild, eggnog-fueled and bold,
Refusing to listen, they gripped tighter their hold.
They clashed in the snow, the night filled with fear,
And the great eggnog riot was far from clear. 

With a flick of his hand, Saint Nick had his fill,
Nick called for reinforcements, quick was the elves will.
The fight was subdued, the damage too much,
And the cadets were left, all bruised by the touch. 

So the officers gathered and made their first call,
And the cadets, once rebels, now all stood tall.
Merry Christmas to all, and to all a good night,
But next time, remember: don’t drink, quarrel, and fight!

To make pasteurized eggs, I heat a sous vide to 135f, and place whole eggs in for 1.5 hours, then chill and use as I would raw eggs in my eggnog recipe. Author: @elviejodelmar2795
Content:
A story please from forgotten military history (well, in truth not very memorable to begin with). The year is 1968. The place is the officer's club of then Ft. Benning, Georgia, the Home of the Infantry. A group of Second Lieutenants in the Infantry Officer's Basic Course were being introduced to tequila. 
One of the group, I admit my guilt, ordered tequila with salt and lemon. The waitress returned with a shot of tequila with a wedge of lemon floating on top and a good shake of salt visible at the bottom. I corrected her but drank my drink. My classmates decided that tequila -- drunk in the correct way -- was the elixir of the gods and the entire group proceeded to get drunk.
The group returned to Olson Hall, the bachelor officer's quarters where junior officers were housed. It is necessary to understand that Olson Hall is immense. It is two stories high and a half mile in circumference. Since we had some foreign students in the class, we decided to conduct the first-ever international laundry cart race, taking advantage of the laundry carts left in the hall by the maids.
At some point (remember the whole episode was blurred by booze) I found myself on the ground floor yelling the jump commands up to the second floor. I finally got a classmate standing in the door balanced on the railing of the second floor, a full twenty feet above the ground.  I yelled, "Go". He lurched a bit, but froze in the door. I repeated the command, and deriding him, yelled "You're airborne aren't you? Go!" He still had enough sense to climb  down.
Fast forward to 1985. The place. Ft. Lewis, Washington. He was a full colonel, the chief of staff to the commanding general. It's a good thing he didn't jump.

Author: @rainbowkeykaraoke
Content:
If you don't want to deal with unmixable nutmeg powder, break (but don't grate) the nutmegs and submerge in the whiskey a week or two before you use it. You can add cinnamon sticks and whole cloves too; these don't need to be broken for their flavor to dissolve into the whiskey. Don't leave cinnamon sticks in for more than a couple of weeks, or the whiskey starts to taste of tree bark.

A heavily spiced version of this is great to add to french toast dipping liquid.

If you want to (have to) do this with grated spices, pour the whiskey through a coffee filter to remove the powder before use.

Content:
If you have a sous vide cooker you can pasteurize the eggs and use the whites safely. They whip very well. 
Preheat the water bath to 135°F (57°C) 
Place the eggs in the water bath, making sure there's enough space for the water to circulate
Cook for 75 to 90 minutes 
Immediately transfer the eggs to an ice bath to stop the cooking process
